content: Mercury poisoning, also referred to as mercurialism or hydrargyria, is a pathological condition caused by exposure to mercury or its toxic compounds. In children, it is sometimes called acrodynia. Mercury is a heavy metal that accumulates in the body and exists in three primary forms: elemental mercury, inorganic mercury (as salts), and organic mercury (as organomercury compounds). These forms differ in their absorption, metabolism, and toxic effects. Regardless of the form, sufficient exposure to mercury can result in damage to the central nervous system, liver, gastrointestinal tract, and other organ systems. Symptoms of mercury poisoning often include sensory impairments such as vision, hearing, and speech disturbances, as well as altered sensations and impaired coordination. The severity and type of symptoms depend on the specific mercury compound, the dose, and the route and duration of exposure. Campaigns in many countries have sought to ban mercury due to its toxicity. Signs and Symptoms Common symptoms of mercury poisoning include peripheral neuropathy, which manifests as paresthesia (tingling or numbness), itching, burning, or pain. Skin discoloration, such as pink cheeks, fingertips, and toes, along with swelling (edema) and skin peeling (desquamation), are also observed. Mercury interferes with the breakdown of catecholamines, leading to excessive epinephrine levels, which can cause profuse sweating (hyperhidrosis), rapid heart rate (tachycardia), excessive salivation (mercurial ptyalism), and high blood pressure (hypertension). Mercury is believed to inactivate S-adenosylmethionine, a compound essential for catecholamine metabolism. In children, mercury poisoning may present with red cheeks and nose, erythematous lips, hair loss, loss of teeth and nails, transient rashes, low muscle tone (hypotonia), and sensitivity to light (photophobia). Neurological and psychiatric symptoms, such as emotional instability, memory impairment, and insomnia, may also occur. The clinical presentation can mimic conditions like pheochromocytoma or Kawasaki disease. Causes and Sources of Exposure Mercury poisoning results from significant exposure to elemental mercury or mercury compounds. Exposure can occur through inhalation of contaminated air, ingestion of contaminated food or water, or direct skin contact. Industrial emissions, particularly from burning fossil fuels like high-sulfur coal, are a major source of mercury pollution. Other sources include mercury mining, smelting, chlor-alkali plants, and the use of organomercurial pesticides. Improper disposal of mercury-containing items, such as fluorescent light bulbs, can also lead to exposure. Mercury vapor is released from crematoriums, waste incinerators, and even natural sources like volcanoes. The consumption of fish is the most significant source of mercury exposure in humans, as mercury bioaccumulates in aquatic food chains. Larger fish species, such as tuna and swordfish, tend to have higher mercury concentrations. Regulatory agencies like the FDA advise limiting consumption of certain fish, especially for women of childbearing age and children. Despite the risks, studies suggest that the nutritional benefits of fish consumption during pregnancy may outweigh the potential drawbacks of methylmercury exposure. Mercury can also be absorbed through the skin, particularly in cases of direct contact with highly toxic compounds like dimethylmercury. This compound is so dangerous that even a small amount spilled on the skin or a latex glove can be fatal within hours. Toxic Effects Mercury is highly toxic to the central nervous system, endocrine system, kidneys, and other organs. It can also damage the mouth, gums, and teeth. Prolonged or heavy exposure to mercury vapor can lead to irreversible brain damage and death. Mercury is particularly harmful to fetuses and infants, as it inhibits the formation of myelin, a critical component of nerve sheaths. This can result in severe neurological consequences. Mercury poisoning has been hypothesized as a potential cause of autistic behaviors, but this theory remains controversial and unsupported by reliable studies. The toxic effects of mercury vary depending on whether the exposure involves elemental mercury, inorganic mercury salts, or organic mercury compounds. Elemental mercury vapor is readily absorbed through the lungs and is highly toxic, whereas its absorption through the skin or gastrointestinal tract is less efficient. Organic mercury compounds, such as methylmercury and dimethylmercury, are extremely toxic and can cause severe brain and liver damage. Dimethylmercury, in particular, is so lethal that even a few microliters spilled on the skin can result in death. Inorganic mercury salts primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract and kidneys, causing severe kidney damage. However, they are less likely to cause neurological damage unless exposure is continuous or heavy, as they do not easily cross the blood-brain barrier. Mercury (II) salts are generally more toxic than mercury (I) salts due to their greater water solubility and absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. Prevention and Regulation Preventing mercury poisoning involves reducing or eliminating exposure to mercury and its compounds. Many governments and organizations have implemented measures to limit mercury exposure, such as banning mercury-containing devices and reducing the use of mercury in industrial processes. For children, efforts focus on limiting consumption of mercury-contaminated fish and removing mercury-containing preservatives like thimerosal from vaccines. Pediatricians are advised to avoid using mercury-containing devices and to educate parents about the risks. Historical and Notable Cases Several significant cases of mercury poisoning have been documented. In Minamata, Japan, from 1932 to 1968, methylmercury was released into the sea, leading to widespread poisoning among the local population who consumed contaminated fish. This resulted in over 1,000 deaths and numerous cases of permanent disability, a condition now known as Minamata disease. In rural Iraq in the early 1970s, mercury-treated grain intended for planting was mistakenly used to make bread, causing widespread poisoning. In 1997, a Dartmouth College professor, Karen Wetterhahn, died after a single drop of dimethylmercury penetrated her latex glove. Other cases include intentional poisoning and historical uses of mercury in medicine, such as in teething powders and intestinal obstruction treatments. Acrodynia Epidemic Acrodynia, also known as pink disease, is a form of mercury poisoning in children characterized by pain and pink discoloration of the hands and feet. It was common in the early 20th century and was later linked to mercury exposure from calomel in teething powders. The prevalence of acrodynia declined significantly after calomel was removed from these products in the 1950s. Mercury in Medicine and Cosmetics Historically, mercury was used in various medical treatments, including as a key ingredient in medicines like blue mass and for clearing intestinal obstructions. While its use in medicine has declined, mercury-containing compounds are still found in some vaccines and dental amalgams, sparking controversy over their safety. Thimerosal, a mercury-containing preservative, has been used in vaccines since the 1930s. Although no adverse effects have been proven, its use has been reduced as a precautionary measure. Mercury is also found in some illegal skin-whitening products, particularly in imported cosmetics. These products can contain dangerously high levels of mercury, which is readily absorbed through the skin. The FDA has issued warnings against their use, as cases of mercury poisoning have been linked to these products. Skin-whitening products are especially popular among Asian women, and some have been found to contain mercury concentrations thousands of times higher than recommended levels.
